question_text: According to the shell theorem, how does a spherically symmetric body affect external objects gravitationally?
option_a: As if all its mass were concentrated at a single point at its center

option_d: With a force that is always weaker than predicted by Newton's law
facts_json:
"• The shell theorem is a classical mechanics principle that provides gravitational simplifications for spherically symmetric bodies, with particular applications in astronomy.

• Isaac Newton proved the shell theorem, which states that a spherically symmetric body affects external objects gravitationally as if all its mass were concentrated at a single point at its center.

• For hollow spherical shells, no net gravitational force is exerted on any object located inside the shell, regardless of the object's position within the shell.

• Inside a solid sphere of constant density, gravitational force varies linearly with distance from the center, becoming zero at the center due to symmetry.

• The theorem was crucial to Newton's analysis of planetary motion and requires calculus to prove, though the results are not immediately obvious.

• The shell theorem applies beyond gravity to any phenomenon following an inverse square law, including electric fields generated by spherically symmetric charge distributions.

• Gauss's law for gravity provides an alternative mathematical framework for expressing the shell theorem.

• The mathematical derivation involves building up from rings to discs to spheres, calculating gravitational fields at each level of complexity."

• **Key legal principle**: The Court ruled that the Higher Education Technical Amendment did not need specific reference to §407 since the 1996 Debt Collection Act already provided the required authorization for Social Security offsets

• **Opinion author**: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor delivered the unanimous decision, with Justice Scalia filing a separate concurrence arguing that express-reference provisions cannot bind future legislatures
